newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: ROTHMANS MAY PROFIT FROM TAX DISPUTE.
newsitem.headline: ROTHMANS MAY PROFIT FROM TAX DISPUTE.

text.p: Cigarette manufacturer Rothmans of Australia Pall Mall (Australia) Ltd could face a lower tax bill than its competitors if industry efforts to overturn a new weight-based tax are unsuccessful, according to industry officials.
The three main producers have presented a united opposition to the new tax, arguing that it will add an extra A$500 million to the industry's A$4.2 billion tax bill.
However one problem for Philip Morris Co Inc's Australian unit and W.D. & H.O. Wills Ltd is the fact that Rothmans' cigarettes are generally lighter than those of its competitors.
"Overall their portfolio of brands is lighter in weight," a Philip Morris spokeswoman confirmed.
"It's fair to say that if the solution adopted was simply moving to straight weight-based tax there is a potential for profit redistribution," said corporate communications manager Nerida White.
The total of the profit changes -- away from Philip Morris and Wills and towards Rothmans -- would be in the order of "tens of millions" of dollars, she said.

Prior to last week's High Court ruling which found state taxes for petrol, tobacco and alcohol unlawful, about 24 percent of the price of a packet of cigarettes came from a weight-based Commonwealth tax and 42 percent from value-based state taxes.
Shifting to a Commonwealth tax system based entirely on weight -- the proposed solution to the problem -- would benefit Rothmans, industry spokesmen said.
"It will make their manufacturing costs lower overall," said W.D. & H.O. Wills public affairs manager Stuart Silver.

Both Philip Morris and Wills, which is a subsidiary of B.A.T. Industries Plc, raised the tax change with the Federal government last week but said the industry's primary focus was on the extra tax impost it faces.
"You might think Rothmans would be in favour of that method, (weight-based tax) but in fact they are not because of the distortion in the market," Silver said.
"You throw all your cards up in the air and the relative stability we have had since the 1995 price war will be disturbed again," he said.
Silver said the pricing of individual brands would also not simply reflect any change to the tax system, but would include other marketing decisions.

A Rothmans' spokesman was not available for comment. The company is about 50 percent owned by Rothmans International Ltd which is in turn owned 60 percent by Swiss firm Richemont AG and 40 percent owned by South African group Rembrandt Group Ltd.
Philip Morris has about 36 percent of the Australian cigarette market, Wills has about 33 percent and Rothmans about 31 percent.
